Yes. And I think the key distinction you're making is not merely “use a registry instead of imports.” You're describing a different compilation/runtime model.

The registry becomes the topological map and interaction boundary, while the individual components remain independently buildable units.

The architecture you're describing

                     │
                     ▼
          ┌─────────────────────┐
          │ Structure Generator │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │

                     │
        ┌────────────┴────────────┐
        ▼                         ▼
   FILE MANIFEST            COMPONENT MANIFEST
        │                         │
        └────────────┬────────────┘
                     ▼
             COMPONENT REGISTRY
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          │          │          │
        hooks      wires       data
          │          │          │
          └──────────┼──────────┘
                     ▼
              COMPONENT ROUTER
                     │
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          ▼          ▼          ▼
       comp-A     comp-B     comp-C
       chunk      chunk      chunk

The important part is the registry exists before the components are implemented.

That gives you a contract to build against, rather than having the components discover each other through imports.

So instead of this
JavaScript
import { foo } from "../foo/foo.js";
import { bar } from "../bar/bar.js";
import { baz } from "../baz/baz.js";

you get something closer to:

JavaScript
registry.resolve("foo")
registry.emit("foo.event", data)
registry.invoke("bar.action", args)
registry.hook("baz.lifecycle", handler)

The component doesn't need to know:

“Where is foo.js?”

It only needs to know:

“I require capability foo.event.”

That's a substantial reduction in coupling.
